summary:
Hygieia, named after the Greek goddess of health, is an onboard health copilot for deep-space crews. On the way to Mars, a flight surgeon can be up to 22 minutes away each way, so astronauts must assess and act on their own health.

Hygieia learns each astronaut’s personal baseline across vitals, sleep, mood, reaction time, vision and radiation dose. It flags drift in plain language and finds the smallest change that brings them back to green, such as “sleep 7 hours for two nights.” An interactive, color-coded body map shows status at a glance. Forecasts predict who is fit for upcoming tasks like spacewalks and suggest trained replacements. Instructions written in advance by flight surgeons trigger onboard instantly. In an emergency, a voice-guided triage mode walks non-doctors through steps up to CPR, with no internet needed, then sends a compressed report to Earth. Profiles adapt Hygieia to a spacecraft, a space station or a surface base.

Every feature maps to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards. The same approach could serve remote communities on Earth, where a doctor is hours away.
details:
Hygieia: onboard crew-health assistant for deep-space missions

What does it do, and how does it work?

Hygieia, named after the Greek goddess of health, is a crew-health assistant that works on board, without waiting for Earth. On a Mars mission the flight surgeon can be up to 22 minutes away each way, so the crew needs answers locally.

It does five things:

  • Learns each astronaut’s own baseline. For every measure (sleep, mood, heart rate, HRV, blood pressure, oxygen, reaction time, radiation dose and more) it keeps a rolling 30-day personal baseline and flags drift as green, amber or red.
  • Explains the drift in plain words. A body map colours each region by its worst measure, and a readiness score from 0 to 100 shows which regions cost points and why.
  • Puts the heart first. Each astronaut page leads with a heart card: resting rate, heart-rate variability, blood pressure and blood oxygen, each compared with that person’s usual values, with a rhythm trace paced at their measured rate.
  • Proposes the smallest way back to green. It simulates levers such as sleep and shared crew time, searches for the lowest-effort plan, and shows the projected recovery day. A slider lets the astronaut try alternatives instantly.
  • Supports decisions and emergencies. It gives go/no-go for upcoming tasks with a suggested trained replacement, and guides the crew through a chest-pain emergency by voice or touch, including a 110 bpm CPR metronome for microgravity. Triage uses no AI and no network.

Houston stays involved through standing orders written in advance and applied on board at once, and a delayed link that queues compressed incident reports. Each astronaut chooses which data categories Earth can see.

What benefits does it have?

  • Earlier warning. Personal baselines catch a change that population thresholds would miss, and a 7-day forecast shows where a trend is heading.
  • Autonomy. Alerts, scoring, triage and standing orders all run on board and offline.
  • Actionable advice. The crew gets one concrete plan with a projected recovery day, rather than a list of abnormal numbers.
  • Safer task planning. Readiness is projected to the task day, so a spacewalk can be reassigned before it becomes a risk.
  • Trust and privacy. Every sourced number links to where it came from, and the private journal is never shared.

What is the intended impact?

In space, the aim is to keep a crew healthy and able to act when help is minutes or months away. Hygieia maps to NASA’s five hazards of human spaceflight and covers NASA’s 17 human-health risks at three honest levels: monitored, self-check only, or knowledge base only.

On Earth, the same engine runs as a Remote clinic profile for communities far from a doctor. It includes an outdoor heat-stress card built on NASA POWER data and an interface in English, French and Arabic.

What tools, languages and data did we use?

  • Languages and framework: TypeScript, Next.js (App Router) and React, with Tailwind CSS.
  • Analytics engine: pure TypeScript, so the same code runs on the server and in the browser. It uses robust statistics (median and MAD), Mahalanobis distance for whole-body anomalies (ml-matrix), Holt trend forecasting, and a grid search for the recovery plan.
  • Storage: SQLite through better-sqlite3 and Drizzle ORM.
  • Charts and visuals: Recharts, plus a hand-drawn SVG body map and heart trace.
  • Browser features: Web Speech API for voice commands, Web Audio API for the CPR metronome, CompressionStream for report compression, and a service worker for offline use.
  • AI: the Claude API for an optional chat assistant; nothing safety-critical depends on it.
    • NASA/CCMC DONKI solar particle events and flares
    • NOAA SWPC GOES proton flux and planetary K index
    • NASA/JPL Horizons Earth–Mars light time
    • NASA OSDR study metadata
    • NASA POWER surface weather
    • Published dose rates from MSL Curiosity RAD, Chang’E 4 LND and ESA DOSIS
    • The Canadian Space Agency’s ISS neutron share
  • Hackathon offers: GoDaddy domain

How is it creative?

  • Path back to green. Most monitors stop at “something is wrong”. Hygieia answers “what is the least I need to change, and by when will I recover?”
  • Real solar storms on the mission clock. Real solar particle events from NASA’s records are replayed on the mission timeline, where they trigger a storm-shelter checklist and show up in each astronaut’s dose chart.
  • Standing orders across the light-time gap. The surgeon’s judgement travels ahead of the emergency, and the alert carries their name.
  • One app, five environments. Switching between Transit, Station, Lunar base, Mars surface and Remote clinic changes the dose rate, thresholds, medical kit, link delay and even the triage steps.
  • Microgravity CPR named correctly. The CPR screen teaches the Evetts-Russomano method with a metronome.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Distance from Earth. Anything urgent must work with no link, so triage and alerts never depend on the network or on AI.
  • Individual differences. Astronauts are compared with themselves, not with a population average.
  • Honesty about limits. Bone loss is inferred from exercise adherence, not measured. The vision check is a screening prompt, not a diagnosis. Under-investigation countermeasures are described as research, never as treatment.
  • Privacy and crew autonomy. Sharing is per category and under the astronaut’s control.
  • Teamwork. Crew goals are cooperative with no leaderboard, because NASA lists inadequate teamwork as a risk.
  • Usability under stress. Emergency screens use huge buttons, few words and voice; status is always a colour plus a word.
  • Provenance. Every figure taken from a dataset or paper links to its source.
